children: Ships approaching Suez from the western Indian Ocean enter the Gulf of Aden through waters framed by Puntland’s Ras Aseyr, historically known as Cape Guardafui, and the Socotra archipelago. This is the Guardafui Channel. From there, the route continues west through Bab el Mandab into the Red Sea.

Bab el Mandab dominates strategic maps because its narrow waters expose shipping to disruption. Guardafui receives attention mainly in studies of piracy and navigation. Yet it poses the larger African question. Who governs the waters approaching the chokepoint, and who benefits from the ports, fisheries, military access and digital infrastructure along its African shore?Africa’s position gives it geopolitical weight. Organised public institutions convert that position into power. A state must know what crosses its waters, decide who may operate there, collect lawful revenue and enforce its decisions. When these functions remain divided, foreign governments, companies and armed networks gain influence over the terms of access.

The struggle over who governs these waters began long before the modern chokepoint. Aden, Zeila, Berbera, Bosaso and Mogadishu once formed part of a maritime economy ordered by African, Arab and Indian merchants through credit, reputation and locally negotiated protection. Britain’s occupation of Aden in 1839, followed by steam navigation and the opening of Suez in 1869, gradually shifted the balance. Imperial navies secured the main routes, while European shipping firms and insurers gained growing influence over the terms of trade. Older commercial networks endured within a maritime hierarchy increasingly defined elsewhere.

The present order carries that inheritance. The Yemen war drew Africa’s Red Sea coast into a strategic network in which Gulf investment in Berbera and Bosaso complemented military access at Assab, linking commercial interests to security objectives without collapsing the distinction between them.

In Djibouti, established and emerging powers used military bases to monitor shipping and support regional operations, while leveraging their presence to expand political influence across the Horn. Their agreements join port investment, military access and diplomatic alignment. Each one allocates revenue, gives practical weight to particular jurisdictions and shapes the choices available to African governments.

For states facing scarce capital and urgent security pressures, these partnerships provide infrastructure, financing and protection. They also give external actors influence over assets that help constitute the state. Ports generate trade and jobs while redistributing leverage among national governments, regional authorities and foreign powers with secure access.

From late 2023, the Houthis showed how armed power projected from one shore could redirect global shipping and alter the regional balance. Drones, missiles and targeting intelligence enabled a land-based movement to raise the cost of passage through Bab el Mandab. By March 2024, traffic through Suez and the strait had fallen by about half. A force controlling part of Yemen’s coast had changed shipping decisions across the world.

For Africa, the disruption brought higher costs and a possible commercial opening. Across East and North Africa, the disruption brought higher freight costs, slower imports, rising food prices and tighter public budgets. The longer route around the Cape also brought business to ports able to refuel, repair and supply passing ships. The rewards were uneven. Carriers charged more, insurers collected higher premiums and traders profited from shortages and price differences. Foreign firms retained much of this value through their command of shipping, finance and risk. Ports with strong inland links kept more of it at home, turning passing traffic into jobs, revenue and lasting commerce.

Somali piracy reveals the security consequences of the same institutional weakness. Naval deployments with the support of Puntland’s forces reduced attacks after 2011, while inland networks retained the capacity to reorganise. Financiers, recruiters, negotiators and political protectors remained embedded across coastal communities and trading centres. As naval attention moved towards the Red Sea, pirates returned with satellite communications and captured fishing vessels used as motherships.

Foreign fishing forms part of this political economy. Industrial and illegal fishing have intensified pressure on fishing grounds and sharpened coastal grievances. Opaque licences, Somali brokers and private protection networks have connected foreign vessels to officials and armed actors. Genuine grievance and organised crime grew together where regulation and enforcement remained fragmented.

Much of East Africa’s connection to global finance and the internet runs through cables laid beneath the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. When several were severed in 2024, banks, businesses and public agencies across the region felt the disruption. A break on the seabed quickly became an economic and security problem on land. The episode exposed a deeper weakness. States dependent on a few routes, with limited repair capacity and few alternatives, remain vulnerable to accident, sabotage and coercion. Maritime sovereignty now includes authority over cable landing agreements, repair access, network information and domestic connectivity.

Africa’s maritime architecture was designed around piracy, trafficking, fisheries and shipping. Cable governance is divided among maritime authorities, telecommunications regulators, security agencies and private operators. Closing that gap requires clear law, shared information, assured repair access, African technical expertise and resilient domestic networks.

For Somalia, that chain of authority must connect the federal government with Puntland State. The Federal Government represents the country internationally and carries responsibility for treaties and foreign military arrangements, exercised through constitutional procedures and federal consultation. Puntland governs the Guardafui coast through its police, fisheries authorities, port institutions and community networks. Their responsibilities converge whenever an external agreement requires enforcement along that coast. A binding maritime protocol should therefore define authorisation, operational command, intelligence sharing, revenue and accountability.

Guardafui brings the stakes into focus. External powers want predictable passage through the corridor. Coastal communities depend on secure access to fisheries and trade. Somali authorities seek effective jurisdiction over both. The institution that aligns rules, revenue and enforcement will shape the maritime order around the Guardafui channel. Africa’s strategic task is to ensure that this power rests in accountable African institutions able to protect the coast, bargain with external powers and turn maritime wealth into national capability.
